Well let's get the date on here first. Well date is the 9th, 30th, 1959
9th month, that's September.
We're at 600 Charter Street.
Back for the second interview. Yeah, and what's your name?
Andrew Bailey, Andrew Bailey. I'm Dick Allen
Bill, what's your name? Bill Russell again. Okay, let's see. You made up a list of questions I got it right here. Okay, let's see. You got something here about the two step on the question.

Oh, the first step is here about the musician. Oh, Chris Kelly? Yeah, Chris Kelly, one of the wonderful conness players, used to play at the Poise Brennan Hall. Come from down the country, which is which is, which is, which is down volley. And he made his home up here in the city. Used to play music at the Poise Brennan Hall. One of the people would yell, tell us they're playing at a concert, and come up there, and everybody looks for him, and they come to the concert, and they yell about the name of the band, which is Chris Kelly. It was a drawing card.
Were those bands, like one will be in one hall and one will be with another, will they try to empty the other hall?

Well, no, they된된된된된된된 된된된된된된된된된된된 main hall which be described for about a month to see a party going on and Chris Keller gonna play and everybody would say well we'll be there and then know we're gonna enjoy ourselves when Chris Keller plays music. Well how would they let you know that Chris was playing? Well we had their appetizers on the program for about a month and then they see who was playing there and most of the people go by the music by the name of the cornet player of the old band that's what they would go by in the olden days the name of the cornet player. Well now these programs
what would they do with the program so that you see them? Well they'd be on doors of
house residents, different section people would read about them that would draw the crowd when they read the program. I see
Let's see. Next you got some old dancers. Yeah some of the old dancers. When Chris

Keller we play in these melodies they likes that rock and roll I mean they likes the ball and jack and the dance called the bucket and shake that thing. Blow the breeze that's the olden time dance. Ain't the dance that has the game. Ain't the dance that has the game. This is uh the lindy hop. The new dancers and all that. The old day they rock the bucket. Ball and Jack.
What was ball and jack like? Was it a special dance? Well yeah well there wasn't no special dance but people would

dance and fella would know it a dance you put your two knees together and you start to dance and just twist your knees you gotta know how to do it. But I used to be in it myself and come down that old ball and jack I was bailed right on the stand to do it. I loved it. Well would one guy get up there? No there would be plenty of them be doing that dance. On the dance floor? On the dance floor. Yeah. Well how do you shake that thing? Well that's a little thing you stand steady. Twist your body. Yeah I see. You don't move your feet then huh? Well you don't move your foot but you stand still and twist your body. What was the eagle rock? Well eagle rock was one of the wonderful days too. Eagle rock. That's a slow drag. You shove your lady out and come back and catch it. Then you go to rocking. The music say ho and they go to rocking. When they say ho they go to rocking. Then you start to

play the music and then you go to swinging. Well you know how a band will be playing along and then everybody in the band will stop and then they'll start up again you know? Yeah. And you continue dancing on.

Keep getting your dancing. Well what do you call that? Well that's like when you when you when you're even rocking it just stops. Everybody stop and say rock. Well it's all stay stuttering. Among the heads they've got ladies friends and they'd be dancing together in one spot just twisting itself. And the music start again then you go on and dance. And you start dancing maybe two steps. Yeah. Now everybody had different signs of dancing. How did the bucket go? Well that's a that's a dance. That's a dance. You be dancing the meeting may say do the bucket. Well you stop and you got a good back well you can just go and do the bucket. But you dance you got to squat down and come up again. How far back do you lean your back on that? Well that's way that's where I'm way back 1920. They had them dances like that. Is that the one where you lean over backwards? What shaking the bucket? Yeah. Well no not shaking the bucket. You lower your go down way to the ground to the floor or more because you're shaking yourself. You got your leg in your hand. Then you come up. Time you come go down slower and you come up the music starts playing fast. Then you start to dancing. You beat and dip your bucket. Do the bucket.

Now out on Mardi Gras day sometimes you know everybody would be loaded and you'd be second lining. and you see people. They get down on their knees and they bend over backwards and they sort of dancing and shaking. What do you call that?
Well some of them get down on their knees they call that uh some of them used to name it the elephant dance. Elephant dance.
Now what about the puppy? What's that?
Well that's the puppy you just have your leg in front of your feet dancing and you're just staying and you go just like a dog running which is in one spot. Well we calls it you're shaking.
Do you move your feet when you do the puppy?

No you need one spot. Well that's about like shake that thing. That's right. Well shake that thing you use your body. Your whole body moving. You're putting one place but your body moving. And the puppy you use your body too? Well the puppy use a part of your body. You got to know how to do them
dances. We ought to take movies for this. We'll do that. Now uh you got here looks like what's that some old

engine? Well that time they had the old horse and horse engine engine. They didn't have the automobile. Them did some of the old time of the engine horses. When they have a fire they had to have horses. The giant man be there at this station all night on their watch. When the fire come they have the harness all up in the adders and they just drop it on the horses and they go to the fire. Ain't no more to the stuff. The olden time. They have some of the beautiful horses you've ever seen in history. In giant horses. Did you ever hear any bands of any fire houses around you? Well no they had no bands no fire houses. And the men had to be on the leash for they work. Yeah well they have that today you know a couple of fire houses. Yeah they don't have that today. Today in giant has everything. Even today I see myself they even do their own cooking. But them days no cooking. Now you got the time of prohibition down here. When was that? Yeah it was in 1915 when the beer went out of existence. They had a local to call the Union Brewery in 161. That's everybody help them out to try to keep beer on. But it didn't exist. It went out of business. That's where the people went to work start to have them speakeasers. Making their own beer selling in hard spots. If you wouldn't know the spot to go in you couldn't get in. When you get in them speakeas you got to talk a lot. Because if you go to talking to the lodge, the lawyer you come in there and make a raise. That's town of prohibition. When that was this 1915. Now what about the river in 1918? You got something about the river? Well that was down in the country there. 1918 was a terrible time. The crow's vest broke. And he even had to get volunteer people to work. Trying to stop the water with sandbags. Keep them coming in the city.
I see. Now what would they do uh at dances? Would they always have a full band of dances?

Well, sometimes they had four pieces of music. Sometimes people wouldn't have all the money to pay for each of the musicians. So they had to get a few pieces of musicians. Sometimes they get a little banjo and a piano player. If you get a four or five people you got the cornet, the clarinet player, and the piano and the drum. Some of them would run out of money and they couldn't have a whole band. But to have a dance you have to have some kind of little music. People like music.
Now what about organ grinders? When would they use it?

Well one time way back around 1916 they had organ grinders. When they wouldn't have money for music there they would get organ grinders. Let them men go around on Friday, Saturday, Sunday. Playing little music from corner to corner. Making their little money trying to make a living. Sometimes they would hire them in a party. That's them grinders. That's them organ that you got to toying. Well how big would those organs be? Well them organs be about, they'd be about a little three feet high. So many inches long fella be pulling it one man to his organ. They had more wheels. They used to, yeah they had wheels on them. They used to rent them organ. You could charge them two niles, two dollars for most all night and bring it on back. But it'd be two dollars rent the margin.
How wide would it be?
Well it wouldn't be too wide. About three or four feet a little wide.
Do you remember some of the pieces they played? What kind of music they had on the organ?
Well they had some of the little, little jazz music. I just remember what kind it was. But they had some nice music. Make you dance, feel happy at it.
Let me see. Do you know the names of any of the organ grinders? Did you know any of them?
Well I had no one little fella used to call Shorty. No short fella. Used to know him. I had another one used to call. Used to call Papa Lewis if he's dead. And them old fella. They gone now.
What about Nicodemus? Did you ever know a fella named Nicodemus?
No I always talk to him but I didn't know him.
Do you know many of these piano players around that just played by themselves?
Well yeah I didn't know right smart of them. This is Virginia Pellibon. Little fella called Sweetie. And this mom I couldn't call their name but I know a very smart of piano players.
Sweetie huh?
Mm-hmm
I wonder if that's the same piano player as in Chicago pal.
No that's this Swedish stage yeah he don't play no more. Still here. Yeah I see him right yeah he don't play no more he's still here.
Fell in Chicago they call him Sweets I think anyway.
Yeah but this little fella called Sweetie but he's still here he don't play no more piano.
Oh while I think of it did you ever hear of a fella they called Papa Deedah Da? No I didn't know. I'm not sure if he was from here or up around Shreveport or up in the Alexander.
This mom I know about eight or ten was piano players I just can't call his name.
I don't know if he was a piano player he might have been a singer entertainer gambler or something else. Yeah I understand. Did you ever heard of him then?
He played Victors Bill. Steve Lewis used to get him out of jail and they played Victors. You did?
Yeah.
He played a piano player Papa Deedah Da. Right across the street there. Steve was the judge and he'd get him out of jail.
Yeah I understand.
You know and get him out of 30 hours for the night and then go back to jail.
Yeah I understand.
Now let me see uh.
Get that list finish that list.
Okay now what about the Ursuline Con then?

Con that's one of the oldest buildings in the United States the Ursuline Street Conway which is the second church in the United States they call it the St. Murr Italian Church where they have and the gym there in the back of the church which they have all kind of entertainment. It's certified entertainment for fights and all that. Concerts, dances be given there.
Now in the old days did they have dances there?
Well they have little dances there.
Now they do huh?
Yeah in the old days they had a few dances there. Always violin players and things. No hard tone music.
What kind of high tone music?
Like violin and what you call guitar. I know banjo guitar. That's the difference in violin.
Any of the other churches have music around?
Well some of them have little concert and thing. Some of the other churches. No Catholic church. But in the Baptist church most have concert.
What about St. Catherine's? Did you ever go by that?
Yeah they had dances. Yeah they had St. Catherine's church. They have dancing because they have a big hall. They have music and everything. St. Catherine's church is a big church where they teach.
St. Catherine's?

Yeah they have a big church there and they have school. Big place for school and they have their own hall. Whenever they have dances they have music. One of them. That's another old church. Old St. Catherine. Still remain on Tulane. And the old Murray there. You remember any of the guys there? No I don't know. I didn't went there a couple of times but I never remember the guys. So you go to these days until you just meet people. Sometimes you just get acquainted with them at that moment. That night.
You wanted to tell us some more about the river Bailey.

Well they had a crovest down down down the river. That was way around 1915. It broke teen. They had to take some volunteers to put sand bags to stop the water from coming in the city. Many people left from down the country. They had to come up in the city. But they floored all the houses away. Chicken and hauls and things. They had to come up in the city. They had to come up in the city. They had to come up in the city.
Uh no I meant about the boats. Guys working. Well the boats. They had a few boats down there.
Some of the old boats would be down there. They called the old Rebben Lee. There's one of the old boats. What's the name of it? Rebben Lee. Robert E. Lee.
Did they have a band on that boat? Did you ever hear of?
Well they had a band but I didn't know the name of it. They had a music and thing. But I didn't know the name of it. You remember that boat? Yeah Robert E. Lee. One of the old boats.
Do you remember ever going on the Sydney or the JFs or any of those boats for an excursion?

Well no I went to one one or two big boats used to go on the excursion. I didn't know the name. It would be a special boat when they would have excursion. Going down to Chalmette. We had to go down to Chalmette. That would be on Armstead Day.
Armstead?

Yeah it's May the 30th. I wish that semester would still remain but it destroyed. Don't use it no more. It has to be a great day Armstead Day. Since it's May the 30th. And like September. First Monday in September used to be Labor Day. And during those days there used to be great days. But I had my old poor dad who was living them days. And he used to have to parade. Which is called the Long Charmette. Nobody would work harder. No working people would wake them days. That's way back. That's way back around 1914. Well it exists up to around 1920. But them old days. They used to have parade. Nobody would work.
What bands did they have on the riverboat?

Well. Well so far the band on the riverboat. They would have a little jazz band when we go down the excursion. You see that old same old man with his pop cellist there. He used to play on them. The only band I know would play on them. Camping down the country as well. They make good. No. Yeah well because you got your door open.
Yeah okay you were talking about their boats.
Yeah definitely. All right well.
Say across the lake. Did you ever go across the lake on the boat?

Well I went across the lake. Well I went to a place from Bay St. Louis to a place to call the Locktown. Right around 1925. When you go to a place to call the Locktown. It was a sawmill I used to work. You had to cross the boat. 12 mile water.
Did they have any blues singers over there in that any camps over there?

Oh yeah they had piano playing and thing. Not much music but plenty of piano playing. Yeah they had nothing but piano. They get in them places they call it the Tonk. See no ball they call it the Tonk. Well what's a Tonk? Well that's a gang of people like in the ballroom they have dancing in the back of the ballroom. That's the name they used to call it. It's a hall but they call it the Tonk. Hunky Tonk. Well they play piano and you go and dance around. Would they have gambling? Yeah some different part from the dancing they had gambling and everything.
What would they play? What kind of gambling?
Well they play all kinds of games. Chord games. Dice, Chord, Koch. All kinds of games they would play. Some would dance and some would gamble and some would drink.
Yeah that's way back. Now what are some of the famous Tonks in New Orleans?
Well I didn't know no Tonk in New Orleans. That was across the lake I went to New Orleans. They had dances in New Orleans.
Did you ever went to Spanos or Kaisers or the Red Onion?
Well that was ballrooms there. Man might have a pen in a ballroom and play like that and you dance. But that wasn't no real dance hall.
But you wouldn't call those places Tonks? They're different.

Well they call them Tonks too. Like all around Old Party Street. All them buildings with them toed on. That'd be Old Tonks they call that. It'd be a ballroom. Or a party Saratoga. Nothing but ballrooms up there.
What were the names of some of the places where they had piano players?
Oh well they had a place called Spanola and called uh oh they had a bunch of them. I just can't call the name at this hour but they had a bunch of them. Yeah.
Red Onion was a famous place.

Yeah. Yeah I was living way down town in the 7 Ward and I used to go up there to call the 3rd Ward from my way out. I feel like taking a little stroll out on Friday instead and call myself enjoying myself. Stop in get one or two little drinks. I'd see the ladies and men be dancing. Piano playing be rolling.
Where was Gasket Street there?
Well Gasket that's right up on a few blocks from Canal Street.
What went on now Gasket Street?

Well they had a boardroom with plenty dancing, gambling, dancing. Some of the places they had fish fries around there. People selling their fish. And their little home brew there them days. Way back around 1919. They had all that.
Well on Gasket Street did they have many women working hustling?
Oh well they had a few of them. They had plenty of them.
Well would it compare with Franklin Street for hustling women?

Well they had them all around there them days. All around there. I was a man I used to go through there but I never just entertain myself and do a little drink going on home. But I never were with the women around there. They had plenty of them. Right small of them. Gasket Franklin, Cyrus, Tilga. Plenty of them.
Did you ever go in the 25s?

Well yeah 25 I went there lately. Way around in 1930. I went in 25. But I was a gamma-fade and it's a dating ballroom. Or you can bring your lady and sit down and drink. Entertain. Might have a piano player but no music. 25 is a gambling place.
What about the entertainers and the ass story?

All that the same. Well that story had music up on top of the building. All that's a lot of them. All that's a lot of them. Upstairs would be for music and entertaining. Dancers would be giving. That's that story. On Rampart Street.
Did they ever go to the Pelican?
Well, Pelican was a little place too. Drinking and things.
Did they have a band of music then?
Well, now and then on Sunday and Saturday and Friday we had little music singing and things. You have to pay to go in them places. It's just about 57.
I was going to ask some more about that lumber camp. Was there a camp over there across the lake where people lived?
Yeah. The fellas lived? Yeah. Well, all them fellas lived over there used to work in sawmills most.
Did they ever move those around from one place to another when they cut the wood? That is, did men follow those saws around?

Well, no, they didn't move the place because there was a big sawmill. The men go in the swamp and bring all them logs. And used to have a big mill where they cut them up and make lumber out of them. I used to work in them myself. I worked in them a while. Until I got sore, I worked in the mill about a month, but the noise was so great for them and making people deep, hard of yearns. I had to quit working in the mill and I got a job on the outside. Driving a cart. What you call a hauling slab for the engine of buying wood. And I stood out there about a year. It was in Locktown, Mississippi.
Well, did these guys ever sing anything when they're driving or working?

Oh, no. You couldn't hear no noise in that mill. No more than the machine. The machine would start at 6 3rd in the morning, wouldn't stop until 6 in the evening. Stop at 12 o'clock for lunch and go back at 1. Just the iron wood.
Did you ever see them saw the trees down or chop them down or whatever that was?

Well, I didn't see them. No, I didn't see them saw them down, but I see them when they're floating in the river and the man be there to come get the logs with them big hooks and put them on their chalk and they bring them to the mill. And they bring them to the mill where they start to sawing them. Make lumber all around the lumber. Make lumber from 2 by 4 and 12 inch planks. All kind of the way they saw the lumber.
Well now, would any of those guys sing like they do on the railroad at all while they were chopping?

Well, not in the sawmill. Too much noise in the sawmill. No, I mean outside. Well, no. They ain't had many outside. Those are the men be in the mill. Waking. I was driving them caught for the sawmill. My car. I used to haul the wood. It was like an ambulance. One day, I'll never forget around 1928, I was in the mill. The mill blowed up and had to get my car to haul the people to the... I wish to call the hospital to the doctor. It was like gambling. The fellow was howling at me. Some of the fellows I would know calling me to print my car. A body here, body there. They blow it up.
How come it blew up?

Well, I guess from the boiler. I don't know what the cause of it. You know what the cause of it. Just blow it up. Some of the people got treated. Crippled. I know it would come up. I would bring them to the doctor. They'd just go on there. I'd just go off and keep a hauling them.
Why don't we let him look over the sheet for the last minute. I don't know if there's anything else on there.

I said you didn't go down the sheet. I think so, but I... Down the river. My refreshments. City said, let's see, party and band was much expensive than the old days. The Ocelain Creek building was the oldest building, charity house in the United States. And the robber will leave one of the old boats to be down the river.
We went over. Yeah, I think we went over that sheet.
Is there anything else you can tell us that you'd like to about the old bands or parades? You say you never followed parades. Did you tell us?

Yeah, I followed parades. Yeah, I used to love parades. Yeah, I used to love parades. I wouldn't know where I'd be at and what war. I would go to it and meet them and get in second line behind the parades. When they go to the parade, they'd be playing some nice songs, hymns. Year of my God the Deeds, sing on. All that kind of music. But when they come from the barren of people, the band starts playing ragtime. Such as you're glad you did, you're gone. It's all kind of music. Ragtime coming back.
Did you ever hear much of the music in the churches, the songs they sang?
Well, I heard a few of them. They didn't have much singing, more than what you mean, in concerts?
No, I mean in the regular church services.
Yeah, yeah, well I heard plenty of them, plenty of music. What would they sing in the church? Well, all kind of hymn. All kind of hymn.
Which religion is this now, Benny?
Well, that's the Baptist.
You've been a Baptist at one time, right?

Yeah, I was a Baptist. I never launched a church, but I always had a Christian heart. But I never been baptized. When you got to get baptized, to see you've been a Christian. If you ain't baptized, you ain't never been no Christian.

Well you weren't born Baptist, huh? Yeah born Baptist but they sprinkled me. They didn't baptize me. They sprinkled me. Some of the people in church, they baptize you. Baptize and sprinkle is different. Baptize they put you in a pool. See in Baptist church they have a pool. They put you down in. What would they sing while they put you in the water? Well they'd be singing and they'd be telling you, well when they be going to put you in the water, they say in the name of the Father, Son of the Holy Ghost, baptize you. Do you believe in everything before you go down that water? When you say you believe in everything, you're all fixed up, got your heart right, they baptize you in the name of the Father, Son of the Holy Ghost. When they put you up out that water, people go to shouting. And what do they shout? Well, redeem. Remember that God redeemed. And when would the singing come on in the church? How'd that work? Well it comes on, God would preach, get you talking, you go to singing.
You don't remember the names of many of the hymns, huh? Well I don't remember the name.
So many names. So many names.
When did you first hear when the Saints go marching in? Did they ever sing that years ago?

No, no. Well I heard it when Louis Armstrong came on the record. Yeah. That's when Louis Armstrong come on the record. They go marching in. You never heard the band play at them before? No, not before Louis Armstrong. Sure didn't. And you didn't hear it in the church? No. Well they used to sing. Used to sing, but I know music. They used to sing. I know music.
Well that looks like about the end of the tape.
Yeah I think that covers that sheet pretty well.
Yeah we just about got all your questions. I hope you can bring your wife.
Yeah I wish she might be a shame. I told her to come. Yeah.
Well she can come and hear this sometime. Yeah. We'll be glad to play it for a baby.
Yeah to me yes.
Alright.

segments.title: Opening: date, location and interview setup
segments.summary: Date, address and speakers are stated; the interviewers go through Bailey's prepared question list.

segments.title: Cornetist Chris Kelly and hall programs drawing crowds
segments.summary: Bailey describes Chris Kelly, a cornetist at Perseverance Hall, and how programs posted on doors advertised bands by the cornet player's name.

segments.title: Old dances: ball and jack, eagle rock, shake that thing, the bucket
segments.summary: Bailey explains how the old dances were done and how the band stops and starts in them.

segments.title: Elephant dance and the puppy
segments.summary: Allen asks about Mardi Gras floor dancing; Bailey names the elephant dance and describes the puppy.

segments.title: Horse-drawn fire engines, Prohibition and the 1918 river flood
segments.summary: Bailey recalls horse-drawn fire engines, the end of legal beer and speakeasies, and sandbagging a broken levee.

segments.title: Small bands at dances when money was short
segments.summary: Dances often used only four or five musicians because people could not afford a full band.

segments.title: Organ grinders: rental, size, music and names
segments.summary: Organ grinders played when there was no money for a band; the organs were rented, and Bailey recalls Shorty and Papa Lewis but not Nicodemus.

segments.title: Local piano players: Sweetie and Papa Deedah Da
segments.summary: Asked about solo pianists, Bailey names Sweetie, who no longer plays, and the interviewers ask about Papa Deedah Da.

segments.title: Ursuline convent hall and church dances (St. Catherine's)
segments.summary: Bailey describes entertainment at the Ursuline convent hall and church halls, violin and guitar music, and dances at St. Catherine's.

segments.title: Return to the river flood
segments.summary: Bailey repeats his account of the broken levee, sandbags and people fleeing to the city.

segments.title: Riverboats, excursions to Chalmette and Armistice Day parades
segments.summary: Bailey recalls the Robert E. Lee, boat excursions with a little jazz band, and holiday parades his father marched in.

segments.title: Crossing the lake to Locktown: honky-tonks with piano and gambling
segments.summary: Bailey worked at a sawmill camp in Mississippi where piano, dancing and gambling went on in the Tonk.

segments.title: New Orleans ballrooms and tonks: Spano's, Kaiser's, Red Onion
segments.summary: Asked about famous tonks in the city, Bailey describes ballrooms and piano playing at the Red Onion on his strolls.

segments.title: Gasquet Street, Franklin Street, the 25s and Rampart Street places
segments.summary: Bailey describes dancing, gambling and hustling women around Gasquet and Franklin, the gambling 25s, and music at the Pelican and on Rampart.

segments.title: Working at the Locktown sawmill
segments.summary: Bailey describes the lumber camp, the noisy mill, his job hauling slabs, and logs floated down the river.

segments.title: No singing at work; the 1928 mill explosion
segments.summary: There was no work singing in the mill; Bailey recalls hauling injured men to the doctor after the boiler exploded.

segments.title: Checking the question sheet
segments.summary: Bailey looks over the list for anything missed.

segments.title: Following parades and second lining
segments.summary: Bailey loved parades, joining the second line; bands played hymns outbound and ragtime coming back.

segments.title: Church singing, Baptist baptism versus sprinkling
segments.summary: Bailey explains his Baptist background, how baptism differs from sprinkling, and the shouting and hymns in church.

segments.title: First hearing When the Saints Go Marching In
segments.summary: Bailey says he first heard the song only when Louis Armstrong recorded it.

segments.title: Closing of the tape and goodbyes
segments.summary: The interviewers finish the question sheet and talk about Bailey's wife hearing the tape.
